newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu turns screws on Arafat.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu turns screws on Arafat.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has turned the screws on Palestinian leadere Yasser Arafat to crack down on militants in the wake of twin suicide attacks in Jerusalem.
The Israeli leader suspended peace talks, launched a wave of arrests, confined Palestinians to their home districts and threatened to re-enter PLO-ruled areas to seize "terrorists" if Arafat refused.
Arafat's aides called the moves a "declaration of war" and said they would only crush Palestinian hopes of peace.
In Washington, members of U.S. President Bill Clinton's Middle East advisory team converged on the White House to discuss how to advance tattered Middle East peace efforts.
A senior State Department official who asked not to be identified said a first official Middle East trip for Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was "an option under consideration."

The pair of human bombs who killed 13 people and wounded 170 at a Jerusalem's main Jewish street market on Wednesday challenged the Israeli leader with the worst civilian carnage in his 13-month tenure.
Netanyahu accused Arafat of having done "damn all" to tackle violence and said the international community had an obligation to demand action from the Palestinian leader.
"You, Mr Arafat...You freed murderers. You yourself incited 'jihad, jihad, jihad' (holy struggle) just a few days ago," a fiery-eyed Netanyahu told Israel's Channel Two television.
"Stop the incitement. Jail the murderers. Find the weapons storehouses and explosives. Act as you are obligated," he said.
By calling off peace talks, Netanyahu broke ranks with the way the left-leaning Labour party predecessors he ousted last year dealt with suicide attacks.
They also launched crackdowns but said halting peacemaking would only allow "terrorists" to achieve their goals.
"Instead of fighting terror they decided to fight the Palestinian Authority," Arafat's aide Nabil Abu Rdainah said of Netanyahu's right-wing government.
World leaders urged the sides to press on with talks.
Wednesday's attack deepened a four-month peace crisis sparked in March when Netanyahu broke ground on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

"Peace can move forward only if the Palestinian Authority and Yasser Arafat undertake what he hasn't done so far and that is a full court press against the terrorists," Netanyahu told Reuters in an interview.

"We have every right to take the actions necessary to defend our citizens and we will do so," he said when asked to elaborate on earlier comments by aides that Israeli forces would re-enter PLO areas if Arafat failed to act.
Israeli and Palestinian security forces arrested suspected Moslem militants in separate raids in the West Bank and Gaza.
In Gaza, Palestinian forces released two senior Hamas political leaders after detaining them for three hours.
Netanyahu said Israel would arrest Arafat's police chief Ghazi Jabali, accused by Israel of organising attacks on Jewish settlers, if he left PLO territory. Jabali scoffed.
"Israel can't arrest me. If they come to Gaza or any place else I am, they will not return," Jabali told reporters. "Do they think that Palestinian people are puppets?"
Officials said Israeli-PLO security meetings took place late on Wednesday in the West Bank but they did not elaborate. They said further contacts were expected overnight.

Israeli pathologists were unable to identify the bodies of the two bombers on Thursday. Security sources said they were not sure of the authenticity of a leaflet issued in Hamas's name claiming responsibility for the attack.

In the West Bank village of Dahariyeh, Israeli forces detained members of two Arab families whose two sons, both Islamic militants, went missing 15 months ago. Forensic experts were checking to see if their DNA matched that of the bombers.

Abu Rdainah insisted the Palestinian Authority was preventing attacks from being launched from areas under its control and warned Israel against "overstepping the red line" by entering Palestinian-controlled territory.
